To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the mil gene is not essential for in vitro transformation by the avian retroviral oncogene myc; (2) in vitro selection for mil gene loss can be overcome by in vivo selection; (3) the mil gene may play an important role in the oncogenesis of MH2 virus; and (4) the v-myc oncogene can be mutated by a process of reverse transcription.

(1) during propagation of the defective retrovirus MH 2, deletions of the genome occur frequently; (2) after transformation of quail in vitro, v mil sequences are often lost from the genome; (3) in contrast, after transformation of quails in vivo, the v mil gene is retained; and (4) MH2-transformed quail cell lines contain deleted proviruses which arose by packaging and integration of the v myc-encoding mRNA.
the mil gene of the avian retroviral oncogene MH2 is dispensable for the in vitro transformation of quail fibroblasts and macrophages and is selected for during in vivo tumorigenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of the viral oncogenes and the mechanism of oncogenic transformation by retroviruses.
understanding the role that the mil and myc proteins play in transformation by the MH2 virus, and with the mechanisms by which the viral genome is modified after infection of quail.
the molecular mechanisms of oncogenesis by avian retroviruses and with the role of the mil protein in oncogenic transformation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mil gene is not required for the oncogenicity or the transforming properties of the MH2 virus.
the v-mil sequence is not required for in vitro transformation of quail macrophages by MH2 virus, but that it is required for the oncogenic potential of the virus in vivo.
the mil protein plays a role in oncogenicity of the MH2 virus, and that the myc protein may play a similar role in the MH2 virus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the v-mil and v-myc sequences of MH2 are not absolutely essential for transformation of macrophages and fibroblasts in vitro, but they are required for transformation of quail in vivo.

the v-mil and v-myc genes are dispensable in the transformation of quail fibroblasts in vitro, but that v-mil is important for the oncogenicity and v-myc is important for the in vitro transforming properties of the MH2 virus in the chicken.
the MH2 virus system is useful in the study of the role of the v-myc and v-mil genes in transformation and oncogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple mechanisms of viral genome alteration that occur in vivo and in vitro.
the mil gene is important for the oncogenicity and transformation of MH2 virus.
there is selection in vivo for the maintenance of the v-myc and v-mil genes.
